subtopic: MR. MARCOUX  STATEMENT BY JUSTICE MINISTER RESPECTING JULES SIOUI

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: MR. MARCOUX  STATEMENT BY JUSTICE MINISTER RESPECTING JULES SIOUI
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege.
As related on page 2761 of Hansard, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau), in reply to a question put by the hon. member for Chapleau (Mr. Laprise) concerning the Indian chief Jules Sioui, answered:
Mr. Speaker, I asked to be informed on the case of Jules Sioui who has been in jail for almost a year and I realized, just by looking at the record, that this case was never submitted to my department.
In all fairness to the Department of Justice and for those who dealt with the case, I must inform the house that I myself instituted proceedings to have Jules Sioui released.
I do not want to insinuate that the minister knowingly misled the house, but I think he was misinformed by his own officials, so that the answer he gave on April 30 last was wrong.
In order to clear up any misunderstanding, I shall read the correspondence I had with the former minister of justice, Hon. Lionel Chevrier, and with the attorney general for the province of Quebec, Hon. Georges-Emile Lapalme.
On June 10, 1963, I wrote the following letter to Mr. Chevrier:
Dear Mr. Chevrier:
On May 10, 1963, Mr. Jules Sioui, an Indian of the Huron reserve, was sentenced to a month in jail for having "maculated electoral lists" placed on the reserve.
And at this stage I should like to inform the house that the Indian reserve is located in my riding. I continue:
The jury had then asked for the leniency of Justice Gerard Lacroix.
Immediately after the sentence, Mr. Sioui expressed his wish to appeal from the judge's decision. He then had to sign a bail enabling him to prepare his new trial before the court of appeals. But almost immediately, a justice employee tore up the signed document.
At the termination of the jail term, on June 6, Mrs. Jules Sioui-a 75 year old woman-went to meet her husband at the Quebec jail. A jail
20220-185i
officer then told her that Mr. Sioui had to post a bond to keep the peace for a period of 18 months. The sentencing document was shown to her.
Mrs. Sioui noticed that the characters in which the mention of bail was written were different from those which had been used for the original sentence.
Mr. Sioui, who was surprised by that addition, refused to sign the document. He has been kept in prison ever since.
And, which is a fact worth mentioning, the letter is dated June 10, 1963. I go on with the letter:
We maintain that he is now illegally detained in the Quebec jail.
I therefore respectfully submit that a request for the immediate liberation of Mr. Jules Sioui is under your jurisdiction.
I trust that your intervention will ensue at the earliest opportunity and remain, sir, yours very truly.
(Signed) Guy Marcoux Member for Quebec-Montmorency
On June 26, 1963, I received from the minister of justice, Hon. Lionel Chevrier, the following letter:
Dear Mr. Marcoux:
I thank you for your letter of June 10 last concerning Mr. Jules Sioui, an Indian from the Huron reserve, near Quebec, who was recently sentenced to a month's imprisonment, after having being convicted of smearing up election lists. The chief electoral officer, as well as the lawyer he appointed to conduct the preliminary inquiry in the Sioui case, informed us that they had' not been aware of the developments mentioned in your letter. On the other hand, I should tell you that when the Sioui case came up for trial, it was in the hands of one of the substitutes of the attorney general for Quebec.
On the other hand, the employees of the various courts of justice are under the jurisdiction of the attorney general of Quebec and the contents of your letter lead me to believe that this is a matter which comes under the jurisdiction of the attorney general of Quebec.
Consequently, and again according to the purport of your letter, it seems to be a case in which my jurisdiction does not entitle me to intervene.
I remain, dear Mr. Marcoux, yours very truly, Lionel Chevrier.
On July 5, 1963, I wrote a letter to the attorney general of the province of Quebec from which I shall read only a few excerpts:
Moreover, I approached the chief electoral officer of Canada, who confirmed the text of the sentence and the fact that the matter was under your own jurisdiction. (He wonders why it should be so.)
I ended my letter in saying:
I respectfully submit, therefore, that it seems obvious that Mr. Sioui is now being illegally confined to the Quebec jail and that you alone can order his immediate release.

Question of Privilege
On July 15, 1963, Mr. Speaker, I had to write once again to the attorney general of the province of Quebec, since I had not received any reply to my letter of July 5. I shall spare the house the reading of that last letter.
On July 16, 1963, I received a letter from the assistant deputy attorney general of the province of Quebec concerning file No. 2323363, in which it was written:
As you mentioned in your letter, on May 10, 1963, Jules Sioui was sentenced to a month in jail for an offence against section 72 of the Canada Elections Act. In addition, he was ordered by the court to provide a $500 bond as a guarantee that he would keep the peace for 18 months.
The judgment passed by Justice Gerard Lacroix stipulates that this $500 bond is to be signed at the expiration of the sentence and that Jules Sioui must not be released until it has been signed.
We are informed by the prison authorities that Sioui refuses to sign the bond on the grounds that he would be submitting to federal authority if he did.
P. Frenette
Assistant Deputy Attorney General
As you can see, Mr. Speaker, that is quite a complicated matter which the Minister of Justice will surely wish to clarify for the house, since we learned just a few days ago that, for no apparent reason, Justice Gerard Lacroix released the prisoner at the end of the period he spent in jail.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not think there is any contradiction between what the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. Marcoux) has just stated on a question of privilege and the reply I gave the other day in the house. This is what I said at that time:
-and I realized, just by looking at the record, that this case was never submitted to my department.
The statement is clear, Mr. Speaker. The accusation was laid under the Canada Elections Act by the chief electoral officer acting on his own. The Department of Justice does not interfere in such cases because the chief electoral officer is responsible to the House of Commons, not to the government. He appoints his own counsel and the case was prosecuted in Quebec city with the assistance of the Quebec attorney general's office, which looks after the administration of justice in that province.
The hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency claims that he intervened in May and June 1963. The situation was brought to my attention and although I knew that I could not intervene directly since the question was outside my jurisdiction, I asked my officials to communicate with the Quebec attorney general's office, since the case was somewhat pathetic in view of the fact that the prisoner refused to help himself. The provincial au-

thorities must have taken the necessary steps, since Mr. Sioui has now been released.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF TRAINING COLLEGE FOR OFFICERS

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Pickersgill (Minister of Transport):
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF TRAINING COLLEGE FOR OFFICERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a statement regarding a matter of policy. For some time the government has been considering the establishment of a training college for new entry officers for the Canadian coastguard. It has now been decided to take advantage of the availability of surplus facilities at the Point Edward naval base at Sydney, Nova Scotia, to get this essential project started. This, of course, will be subject to the provision of the necessary funds by parliament.
In recent years the work of departmental ships has expanded from the maintenance of aids to navigation and some local surveying and icebreaking to a whole range of marine activities. This fleet now mans the weather stations in the north Pacific ocean, covers Arctic supply convoys, escorts the increasingly important winter traffic into east coast ports and the gulf of St. Lawrence, supports scientific work afloat, and provides a special rescue service.
Including ships now building, the coastguard will have grown in 15 years from 27 to 60 ships, plus some 150 large work boats, tugs and barges. The modern units in this growing fleet are increasingly complex and costly, and they are required to operate in situations of special hazard.
Up to the present the department has relied on the maritime industry to provide officers for this important fleet; but the expanding need for officers has been met by drawing on sources that cannot be tapped again, such as the former Canadian National

West Indies service, other flag transfers and direct recruiting abroad. These sources have not provided many Canadian recruits. The efforts of existing marine schools in various parts of Canada are directed mainly toward meeting local needs of a less complex nature.
To the extent that schools such as the marine school at Rimouski, Quebec, and the new college of fisheries and navigation at St. John's, Newfoundland, and other local institutions can meet the standards and syllabus requirements of the new college, arrangements will be made for cadets to take basic training in navigation and other agreed portions of their course at these institutions. This plan will prevent duplication of resources and enable the new college to concentrate on needs that cannot be met in existing schools.
In view of the critical shortage of new officers for the coastguard anticipated in the next few years, it is the intention of the government to proceed with the establishment of the Canadian coastguard college as quickly as possible, as soon as parliamentary approval has been received. Specific entry requirements and other related information will be made public as soon as the detailed arrangements can be worked out. The first step will be to find a suitable director and recruit the staff.
It is not anticipated that actual training will begin until some time in 1965, but I thought it desirable to make this statement at this time as some steps must be taken almost immediately at Point Edward, and I knew the anxiety there was in all parts of the house to make use of these facilities that are no longer required by the navy.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure the house is very grateful to the minister for making his statement at this time because some of us may be a little busy tonight at the time of the C.B.C. newscast. I am very glad to hear the minister make this announcement covering something which is part of a general plan that was established by the previous government.
I think all hon. members know that great services are rendered to our country by the coastguard. Its fleet is an excellent one and very often operates under very strenuous circumstances off the shores of Canada. It is playing a major role so far as Canada's trade is concerned, and in the past has played a major role in very dangerous rescue operations. While I was minister of transport I had the pleasure of presiding over the modernization of the fleet and over a few changes made in it. Its vessels are now painted differently. All the ships are very
Canadian Coastguard
easily distinguishable, and uniforms have been issued to the various members of the fleet.
I am sure this college will meet a need and will give opportunities to young Canadians to find good careers in the Canadian coastguard service. The choice of Sydney is excellent, specially when one thinks of the great naval tradition of this great Canadian seaport.
There is one point the minister has not mentioned. I hope this school will be bilingual, because the great majority of the officers and men serving on these ships come from the shores of the St. Lawrence, and this would be a good opportunity for young Canadians to learn our two national languages.

Mr. Speaker, the members of this party welcome the minister's announcement that a coastguard college is to be established at Point Edward naval base in Sydney, on Cape Breton island. The need for such an institution has been well known for a long time, and I think this will help fill that need. With the curtailment of some of the naval installations across Canada many of the Royal Canadian Navy personnel might be suitable persons for officers in the coastguard, and this should be a very fertile field for recruitment of people to serve in the Canadian coastguard.
We are particularly pleased that the government has selected Point Edward naval base at Sydney, Nova Scotia, for this purpose. All of us who are familiar with conditions in Cape Breton know of the serious unemployment situation that was likely to take place as a result of the closing of Point Edward naval base. If this helps to meet that unemployment situation I am sure it will be welcomed by members in all parts of the house, and that it will be particularly gratifying news to people in the Sydney area. speakeroldname: Mr. John N. Turner (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: FAILURE TO DEVELOP CANADIAN WATER RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last evening when the gong sounded I had described the amendment moved by the hon. member for Brandon-Souris as a partisan attempt to hold the present government accountable for the consequences of a water policy which has been pursued since confederation. I had analysed parts of that amendment dealing with low water levels, increasing pollution and the necessity for conserving water. In the time that remains to me this afternoon I should like to deal with that part of the amendment criticizing the government for failing to establish what is called a co-ordinated national water policy.
I should like to point out to the house that there are grave constitutional limitations attached to that amendment, and that no federal government could be held wholly accountable since it would not have the constitutional power to prosecute a co-ordinated national water policy. Within those terms, I am sure the hon. member for Brandon-Souris must have been aware that the amendment could not withstand constitutional scrutiny. The amendment condemns the government for failing, as I said, to establish a co-ordinated national water policy, and this clearly assumes that the federal government has the constitutional power to establish such a coordinated policy.
Surely, Mr. Speaker, it would be ridiculous to criticize the federal government for failing to do something it did not have the legal power to do. Surely it would be rather frivolous to criticize the federal government for failing to do something it does not have the legal power to do, and failing to fulfil

the proposals in the amendment. I say, therefore, the mover of the amendment completely ignores the constitutional position. The fact is that apart from specific federal powers in relation to navigation, and other limited areas, the water resources belong to the provinces and come under provincial jurisdiction. In that event the amendment has no constitutional footing feet.
The question was very thoroughly dealt with by the resources for tomorrow conference which the hon. member for Brandon-Souris mentioned in his opening address. Professor Bora Laskin, professor of law at the University of Toronto, had this to say about the water supply of the country at the resources for tomorrow conference, as recorded at page 215 of volume I of the conference papers:
It is a safe generalization that the regulation and distribution of water resources in a province for domestic consumption or industrial purposes are within exclusive provincial competence. While some qualification has to be made, as for example, in respect of public rights of navigation or in respect of interference with federal property or competent federal law, it yet remains true that appropriation of water for private use is subject to definition by provincial law.
The constitutional position, of course, does not mean that the federal government has no responsibility and can do nothing. Clearly it must be part of its general responsibility for the welfare of Canadians to take an interest in policy and measures with respect to water, and to assist in its conservation and wise use. Much has been done over the years by the federal government, and by the federal government and provincial governments in co-operation, and I trust I dealt with this aspect in some degree last night.
But what the federal government cannot do is precisely what this amendment implies it should do; that is, exercise federal jurisdiction over a co-ordinated national water policy. In my submission, Mr. Speaker, that is beyond the jurisdiction of any federal government. But a federal government can try, as the present administration is doing to encourage provincial co-operation and concert action by and with the provinces.
Last evening I described the measures this government has taken-

maintopic: FAILURE TO DEVELOP CANADIAN WATER RESOURCES
speechtext:
I have not much time. I am limited to ten minutes this afternoon, but if I have time at the end I will be glad to see to the hon. member's question.
What the present administration has done is to encourage a co-ordinated national water policy, but in co-operation with the provinces under the Canadian council of resource ministers. Recently the Prime Minister announced
Canadian Water Resources the establishment of a provincial relations secretariat to improve co-operation with the provinces, and in our federal system the manner of approach must be by co-operation with the provinces which have the constitutional jurisdiction over water.
That being so I think we can say the present administration recognizes, as the author of the Royal Bank of Canada monthly letter of December 1963, in an article entitled "Saving Our Watersheds" says:
Water is so important in life that its conservation and distribution must override the geographical boundaries of private property, counties and provinces; the political boundaries of federal and provincial jurisdictions, and the economic domains of agriculture, forestry and industry. If jurisdictional disputes prevent effective action, our heritage will be lost by default, because above all boundaries is the supreme natural law whose edicts are indisputable.
That is so, but we have a constitutional limitation which the hon. member for Bran-don-Souris has failed to recognize. In answer to that I would make reference to the arguments that I attempted to bring before the house last evening, that over the last 12 months this administration has used the only consultative constitutional avenue it could. It has brought water control, use, distribution and sewerage before the Canadian council of resource ministers where, in conjunction with the provinces and the regional authorities, this government intends to fulfil its responsibilities within the limitation of the jurisdiction given to it by the British North America Act.

maintopic: FAILURE TO DEVELOP CANADIAN WATER RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to offer congratulations to the hon. member for Brandon-Souris for bringing the very important question of water conservation to the attention of the house; also to the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka for pointing out the great problem we have, and also to the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, who dealt with the problem and gave the previous government credit

Canadian Water Resources for building the Saskatchewan dam, for the resources for tomorrow conference and for ARDA. One of the things he omitted to mention was the help it gave for the building of sewage disposal plants across Canada.
The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George raised the constitutional issue as an excuse for not doing anything. This put me in mind of what Nero did many years ago, when he fiddled while Rome burned. We in Canada have been slow in recognizing that water is one of our great natural resources, that men cannot live without it and that industry and the economy of the country cannot advance without it. In the great lakes area we have many tourist operators who will suffer severe financial losses as a result of the low water levels in the great lakes. Motel and hotel operators all around this area will lose millions of dollars in business because of the low levels, and many of them will be forced completely out of business.
For months hon. members of the house have been drawing this to the attention of the government but there has been little or no realization on its part that it interprets the facts as they exist; or, if there was a realization, it did not know how to meet the problem. We pride ourselves on having half of the available fresh water in the world right here in Canada. We feel it is inexhaustible, but when shortages occur all we do is pray for rain or else wait for the cyclical periods that bring it back up.
I remember it was said that the six or seven year cycle would correct the present situation. Well, the seven year cycle has ended and the situation has not been corrected. In fact none of the cycles will completely correct this problem of low water levels in my riding. The quantity of water in the world remains the same, and we must not forget that fact. It is when the quantity is out of balance that we have problems, and today we have those problems on the great lakes.
Average annual rainfall in the lake Huron-Georgian bay area ranges between 30 inches and 35 inches, but if you take the figures that were given in the house yesterday and add them up, you find that the average rainfall in that area over the last 12 years was 31 inches, and in the same period of time the high water mark has fallen six feet from the average.
This would indicate that precipitation has only a minor effect. It has been said "Leave it alone. It will right itself. It is a gradual process". Well, this gradual process is going to spell financial ruin for many of the operators in our tourist industry, and a lot of them have every penny they own invested in this

business, a business which in the long run brings many millions of dollars to this country. It is, I believe, the third biggest industry we have.
We have been told "Just wait for seven years and it will be all right". Those years have come and gone. I want to read a comment made by Mr. James Lamb, the publisher of a paper in my area. He is well acquainted with the great lakes. This article was reprinted in the Toronto daily Star of May 1, 1964. Mr. Lamb had this to say:
While the great lakes run steadily down the drain, with long established ports now high and dry and Georgian bay down four feet from normal, there is not a man, or a group of men, in Canada or the United States, who has any real idea of cause or cure.
For the shocking truth is that each of the regional developments which has affected the levels of the system has been considered separately, with lake and river problems being attacked piecemeal, rather than in one over-all program.
This, from the same article, is also striking:
One of Canada's best qualified experts on waterway development admitted to a private gathering last year that neither he nor any other engineer or official had any conception of the ultimate effect on lake levels of such revolutionary undertakings as the construction of the St. Lawrence seaway, with its enormous alterations in the flow and depth of the river; of the huge additional diversions at Niagara and Chicago; of the deepening of the channel at Sarnia.
The writer goes on to say:
If this is so, then surely it is time the two federal governments concerned-
The United States government and the Canadian government.
-instituted an over-all lake control system, and took steps to conserve what water is left before lake Huron is reduced to a fraction of its former size, and the lower lakes bereft of half their ports.
For years now official reaction to public complaints about the alarming drop in lake levels has been to place the blame on dwindling rainfall. I have shown that the amount of precipitation is a minor factor having regard to the situation as we know it. Let us face a few facts. More water is being used by householders. A man said to me the other day, in our house "A few years back we used four to six pails of water a day; now, to get breakfast over and everybody up and washed, we use more than that". Today the average person in many of the cities of Ontario uses 100 gallons a day, a striking figure. Industry uses tons of water today whereas a few years back it was using gallons by comparison.
The second point I wish to make is this. We are not conserving the run-off from our lakes and rivers. The obvious conclusion is that dams must be built, because the experts say there is enough overflow from the St. Lawrence run-off to look after all the water needs

Canadian Water Resources
of householders of the rest of Canada for a whole year. If that is true, it follows that the run-off into the lakes and rivers flowing into the great lakes basin is very important and that we must consider what can be done in this respect, in conjunction, of course, with the provinces. However, the great lakes are run by the Department of Transport. They are responsible, and this government is responsible. When this matter was brought to the attention of the government last fall they should have moved quickly to call a conference and clear the way for action of some kind.
The question of water conservation is being approached from other directions. The province of Ontario has recognized the existence of this problem and will allow to farmers 50 per cent of all expenses incurred in the construction of ponds. The previous government recognized the problem when we established a reforestation program under ARDA. This program will give us big sponges of reforestation and ponds to hold the water in many of these areas. Then of course there is the Chicago diversion, which takes about 2 per cent of the water out of the great lakes.
The fifth point I wish to make is that we already have a control on lake Superior; we have a dam. On the other hand, we have no control on lake Huron and Georgian bay. In addition, the area around Sarnia had to be dredged in connection with the building of the St. Lawrence seaway.
The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George put some figures on the record in this debate regarding slower flow. I want to say this. The river St. Clair is flowing faster than ever. When this channel was lowered by six feet the official pronouncement was that the effect would be negligible. Just how this can be reconciled with the actual increase in outflow from 160,000 cubic feet per second to 185,000 cubic feet per second has not been explained. That completely repudiates the arguments put forward by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George.
I wish to dwell for a minute on this increased output of the river St. Clair, taken in conjunction with the fall of six feet in the level of the great lakes in the Georgian bay area. If we are to control lake Superior we must have some control on lake Huron. I think this is definitely indicated when the outflow is 25,000 cubic feet per second more than it was prior to the dredging and deepening of the St. Clair river. It follows that this government must get busy at once, in conjunction with the government of the United States and the international joint commission, to find a solution to this problem and a means of lessening the immediate
difficulties. This should be done, too, in cooperation with those people in Michigan and elsewhere who are vitally concerned.
The government already has the machinery to use if it wishes to get to work on damming the lakes and rivers which flow into this area. I am most concerned about this matter.
I am wondering what responsibility the government must accept for the position in which these marine operators, hotel operators and others on the great lakes find themselves. These people have invested thousands and thousands of dollars from their savings. Many of them have mortgages and they are likely to lose their property in this great catastrophe.
I am wondering whether the government has not some responsibility to those people for the losses which will be incurred. I am not saying that the government should subsidize or should look after all of those people, but I am saying that many of these young operators, on the strength of making Canada one of the great tourist centres of the world, have invested their all, but they find their docks are today six to seven feet out of water. Although they were erected to be of proper height at high water level they are today standing stark naked six to seven feet above water level. You would find, Mr. Speaker, that some of the channels in that area cannot be traversed by boat and tourist places are completely isolated. It does not seem fair to me that we should expect those people to accept the responsibility for this disaster in its entirety, and I hope the government will give serious consideration to providing some form of assistance to these people who, as I say, may lose their all.
Some of the papers in the area, including the Midland Free Press and the Angus Times, have pointed to the distress which is going to be caused in this connection. I know that the government is going to dredge all the harbours and is going to dredge the harbour at Midland and Port McNicoll and Colling-wood. But in the meantime, although ships are carrying lighter loads they are getting bogged down. These boats have to be pulled off mudbanks and so on, and this is costing the economy a great deal of money. Therefore I would appeal to the government to stop this laissez faire attitude which is prevalent today, and get busy and do something for these people, because over their property today rests the pall of loss. We in the house may regard such matters as affecting only one part of Canada, but I suggest that this goes deeper and affects the prairies and the whole economy of Canada. Instead of talking about cycles and other matters it is high time the government did some sound thinking, set up some machinery, put it to work, and

Canadian Water Resources considered the problems and financial losses of the people who live in those areas.

speakeroldname: Hon. Arthur Laing (Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: FAILURE TO DEVELOP CANADIAN WATER RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when my predecessor moved his amendment yesterday I think he took a great many people by surprise. Indeed, I am of the opinion that he took a great many members of his own party by surprise, judging by the participation of hon. members on the other side of the house in this debate. I was certainly taken by surprise. I wanted at once to thank the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) for his generous statement that he "cannot hold it against this new government and the new minister in his first year". I wanted to thank him for that statement, but I hope to be able to prove in the few minutes I am going to take today that we do not need his generosity. Because I think I will be able to point out that we have undertaken a larger number of measures in regard to the full use of Canadian resources in this past year than were ever undertaken for quite a few years prior hereto; and some of the measures we have taken have been relatively successful.
The very splendid speech made by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Turner) was, I think, quite encompassing in that he pointed out the limitations, the very real limitations, which exist in this particular field. I am sure my hon. friend from Burnaby-Coquitlam, among others, is aware of them because at one time he was the head of a provincial government. In the field of resources our provinces are extremely jealous, and of course understandably so, because they derive their revenues from the resources which have been developed within their boundaries. We are now in a position where, to the great advantage of the nation, and I would think, in the end, to the great advantage of each individual province, we are trying to establish a mutuality of interest which does not know provincial boundary lines.
In that respect I think that one of the better jobs which we did last year was as a result of a metting which was held in Regina, which I attended together with a number of members from both sides of this house. We received, I think, a good education apart from having an interesting time. We had been invited there by the premier of Saskatchewan to meet resource representatives not only from Saskatchewan but Alberta and Manitoba as well. Out of that meeting an advisory committee was set up which has since held no less than five meetings. The political end delegated its responsibility to the technical men in the 
various departments. This is all leading to a request which will be made of this government for a very considerable study of the possibility of bending some of these northern rivers into the Saskatchewan system and of diverting some of the waters which today seem to flow uselessly into the Arctic across the prairies where they will be of more value.
Canada is a fortunate country with respect to water in that 7 per cent of its total land mass is covered by water. Of the tremendous amount of water which is annually drawn up by the sun from the ocean and dumped on Canada no less than 8,000 billion tons of it is dumped on the land in the form of rain or snow. Therefore we in Canada are exceedingly fortunate, as I say, in our water resources; our job now is to redirect these resources before they return to the ocean. This involves a tremendous job for the future but we are making a move in that direction.
Certain hon. members on the other side of the house, particularly those down in the corner, have for years been asking about water pollution. We have written a letter to the resource ministers suggesting that the question of the pollution of our waters should be one of the first subjects to be dealt with at the plenary conference of resource ministers when they meet in Charlottetown. This suggestion has been agreed to. We have received affirmative replies from five or six provinces, only the province of Nova Scotia being of the opinion that this is a matter of provincial rather than federal-provincial jurisdiction.
We are also moving in the direction of a very complicated, extended and what will be a very expensive study of the resources of the Nelson river in the province of Manitoba. This study is designed primarily to assist the ultimate development of power, in which more than the province of Manitoba is interested, quite apart from the interest of the government of Canada. This study will be extremely extended and, as I say, very expensive. This is evidence of co-operation with the provinces to develop to the best advantage their resources, to the benefit not alone of the individual province concerned but of the nation as a whole. For example, where rivers cross provincial boundaries it is quite possible for one of the provinces concerned to take action within its provincial borders which would prove extremely harmful, if not disastrous, to its neighbour. There is an increasing appreciation of that situation at the present time and we find the provinces are discussing this matter more and more with one another.
I indicated to the ministers concerned, as recently as January 8 last, the need for the expenditure by us of a great deal more

money in studying the water resources of Canada. Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, I may be permitted to quote one paragraph from that letter, which was sent to all the resource ministers of the provinces:
Recognizing the accelerating needs for water data to enable the responsible agencies to plan for efficient use of our water resources, the government of Canada has agreed to an intensified five year program of expansion and improvement of surface water and sediment survey data collection and analysis facilities by the water resources branch of this department. It is my hope that under this program and through the existing cooperative arrangements with the provinces, we can at least double the existing coverage in the next five years, as well as improve present installations.
We have received replies from the ministers concerned, I think in every instance offering their greatest co-operation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are faced today with a motion which condemns us for our inactivity. I wish to tell the house that we are not inactive, but this particular branch has been extremely active in the last year. In addition it is suggested we are negligent because we have failed to establish a national advisory committee. The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Turner) pointed out some of the difficulties in this regard. We will have it as time goes on, and I would say that we will have it through the means we are attempting to effect at the present time; that is, by working with the provinces and encouraging their support and co-operation. But the condemnation is that we had not established a national advisory committee.
Reference was made by the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale) to the proposal made by the present Leader of the 20220-1861
Canadian Water Resources Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) on October 23, 1961, in which he declared that such a committee should be established. I merely want to point out that the government of that day remained in power for some 18 months thereafter and did not establish such an advisory committee. The difficulties are apparent. However, with the establishment of the secretariat to the resource ministers conference now operating out of Montreal we will be able to achieve the same type of co-operation with the various provinces and, in the end, the same objectives that might be achieved by suddenly setting up a national advisory committee in respect of these matters.
I want to say something in particular about the great lakes system, to which so much time was devoted by the hon. member for Simcoe East (Mr. Rynard). I am fully aware of the deep concern in this respect and of the consequences of a cycle of weather which again is becoming apparent to this region. I say it is a cycle of weather because I had gone back to February 28, 1956, when these remarks were made in the house by Mr. Murphy, the then member for Lamb ton West:
I was not concerned about the effects of the St. Lawrence seaway project on the great lakes levels.. .My concern was about the damage to property from high water levels even at the present moment.
That was in the days when members of parliament were rising in the house and saying that the government had to do something, had to make some release of water somewhere and get the water down the St. Lawrence river because of the damage being caused in the lakes by high water. This is a situation that has been evident to those who have been keeping records over a great number of years. We do have times of heavier precipitation, with resultant damage from floods. I want to tell the house, Mr. Speaker, that the situation in respect of the great lakes system is a very, very complex one; indeed, it has been declared to be the most complex system in the world.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: FAILURE TO DEVELOP CANADIAN WATER RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for his question but I have to tell him that in a circumstance such as we are suffering from it is necessary to impose as little loss as possible on each person. The tendency is to reduce water here, to effect a little damage to shipping, shall we say, in one instance and yet do as little damage as possible. In other words, it is spread all around. This is a situation with which we in British Columbia are familiar. In 1958 I watched the
2934	HOUSE OF
Canadian Water Resources water rise to within six inches of the dike tops at Creston. Creston had been flooded once before. That particular year we saved the Creston dikes, but the Americans lost out down below. There was another occasion on which we and the Americans down below were co-operating to try and save both. We saved theirs but we lost the dikes in Creston. It seems to me this is a case of making the maximum use of water for all purposes and bringing to bear as little damage on individuals as possible.
I have been accused of being flippant because on one occasion I said that prayer might help. I still think it might help. I want to say that at the present time we have a most abnormal situation in British Columbia. I do not want to be an alarmist, but those of us who are members from the province of British Columbia will admit right now that in the next few weeks we are going to go through very trying times in that province. This will not be for want of moisture, some of which I would have hoped we could make available elsewhere, but because the other day, not in northern British Columbia but on the coast in central British Columbia, I flew over an area that is carrying 75 feet of snow; and in parts of the Columbia watershed today-I visited the area some six weeks ago-there are places in which the snowfall has been recorded as being 40 per cent above that of last year. We are hopeful that we can get by, and I think possibly we will; but we have had cool nights lately. This is a situation over which we have as yet, as is the case with most governments of the world, no control. There may be scientific weather controls in later years, but we do not have them yet.
The great lakes is a particular case in point, because the area of drainage into the great lakes is only 201,000 square miles, whereas the great lakes themselves cover
95.000	square miles. Here again the difficulty that occurs is that there is a different ratio of drainage area in the case of each of the lakes. In the case of lake Superior it has a drainage area of only 48,000 square miles for
31.000	square miles of lake. In the case of lake Michigan it has 95,000 square miles of drainage area against 45,000 or about two to one. In lake Erie it is 30 to 10 and in lake Ontario there are 27,000 square miles of drainage area for only 7,500 square miles of lake. So that in this complex pattern with these enormous variations even the arranged feeding of water would be most difficult, costly and time consuming in that you might have to start the water 18 months ahead of the time it would flow out the other end of the lakes. These are complicating factors of the great lakes system.


We are fully aware of the consequences of the present situation. We have been keeping in communication with the Americans on all these points and any of those man-made things to improve the situation which are possible at this time will be done by us from time to time in full co-operation with the Americans.
Again I want to say that in these circumstances the total accomplishments of man, compared with nature's count for very little at all. Those members of the house who are familiar with the situation will agree with me, I think, on the figures I am about to quote in respect of wheat production in the province of Saskatchewan. Last year, under ideal circumstances both in respect of volume and quality, the province of Saskatchewan produced 493 million bushels of wheat. I think it is also absolutely accurate that in the year 1938 the province of Saskatchewan produced 29 million bushels of wheat. It was not because the soil was poorer then than it is now. New methods of soil culture are being used and I rather think that members from Saskatchewan will confirm the fact that there was more fertility in the soil then than there is now. But what was lacking, of course, was water.
We are subject to these circumstances and must do the best we can with them. We have made very good progress in a great number of fields in dealing with the provinces. We are budgeting for over $2 million more for the water resources branch alone this year than the year before, but I must be fair and point out that about $1,300,000 of that amount represents additional sums of money paid in respect of the Winnipeg floodway over those spent the year before. But we are spending more money. We are taking on more staff, and we have been very successful in working more closely with the provinces on the matter of resources that lie within their own boundaries.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise for the purpose of discussing particularly the subamendment, and then I will make some references to the speech of the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Laing) which in my opinion represented a completely negative and defeatist attitude on the part of the government. Because of the fact that there is a subamendment I wish to read the amendment moved by the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale).
This house condemns the neglect of the government in failing to establish a co-ordinated national water policy and in ignoring the imminent national crisis in water resources management, which is evidenced by the critical low water levels of the great lakes and other national waters, the increasing pollution of national waters, and the urgent necessity of conserving water resources. ..
And urges the government, in the interests of national development, to take immediate action...:
(1)	establishing a national advisory committee on water resources...
(2)	accelerating the application of ARDA policies to the problems of national resource development, and,
(3)	vigorously continuing and expanding the water and other resource development programs conceived and established by the previous Conservative government.
The subamendment moved by the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire) simply removes from the amendment moved for the official opposition most of the effective terms thereof. It entirely ignores the national crisis in water resources management. It entirely obliterates the necessity for the establishment of a national advisory committee on resources. Indeed, it emasculates the amendment and substitutes therefor one matter:
That in the best interests of national development, the house urges the government to take concrete steps immediately to accelerate the application of ARDA.
Canadian Water Resources
We can concur entirely with the particular item in the subamendment and its objective, but if we were to vote for it we would be removing the major portions of our amendment and, indeed, would defeat the purpose for which our amendment was moved. As far as ARDA is concerned, which was established under a Conservative government, it is one of the most forward, one of the most effective programs ever enunciated in legislative form in the history of our country. It was entirely in keeping with the general attitude of the Conservative party, whose basic principle is to conserve these things that are good.
The Bennett government brought into effect the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act which, in my province of Saskatchewan and the adjoining prairie provinces, brought about advances that were not even thought possible. The minister referred to wheat productivity in Saskatchewan in 1938. I recall the days of the dust bowl, the frightfulness of which cannot be translated into terms understandable today. Out of the experience of that drought era from 1929 or 1930 to the latter part of the thirties, there was born the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, and through P.F.R.A., changes and improvements have been made.
There is no doubt at all that if we were to accept the subamendment we would defeat the purpose for which the amendment was moved. Since the subamendment does remove the major portion of the material part of the amendment moved by the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale), we cannot support the subamendment moved by the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire). We think that in the best interest of national development the government should take concrete steps immediately to accelerate the application of ARDA. We believe that this government has dragged its feet on the ARDA program. Indeed, as one reads the evidence that was taken before the committee of the Senate on land use in Canada, one cannot but conclude that there has been a total lack of initiative and effort on the part of this government in carrying out the basic principles of ARDA.
This plan was a great step forward for soil and water conservation, and it has been left practically unimplemented, except in a comparatively minor degree. I am not going into the particulars in this regard, but they are set forth in the No. 2 report of the committee to which I referred a moment ago. Incidentally when so much is said by way of criticism of the other place, the work done by the committee under the chairmanship of Hon. Arthur Pearson and the deputy chairmanship of Hon.

Canadian Water Resources Austin Taylor, has been worthy and commendable indeed. The information assembled by the committee, if used by the present government, could extend beyond one's imagination the benefits of ARDA, were that the desire of the government. When I look at what has happened on the western prairies I think of the words of Jeremiah when he said:
And I brought you into a plentiful country, to eat the fruit and the goodness thereof; but when ye entered ye defiled my land, and made mine heritage an abomination.
This applies to what we have done. We have been wasteful and destructive of the great resources we have in our country. In the years ahead, 30 or 40 years from now, water will be more valuable to Canada if we maintain its purity than many of our other resources. I believe it was a great United States political philosopher who said that within 50 years water will be a more valuable resource than oil itself.
The minister always speaks delightfully and in the best debating traditions of parliament. I enjoy listening to him. However, at the conclusion of his remarks today I could not but conclude he realized he did not have any case, and therefore he had to speak in that kindly way that always characterizes him when he realizes he has a difficult, if not impossible, task.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: FAILURE TO DEVELOP CANADIAN WATER RESOURCES
speechtext: Others shout loud.

maintopic: FAILURE TO DEVELOP CANADIAN WATER RESOURCES
speechtext:
Yes, and the minister never shouts because he has nothing to shout about. I am glad he interrupted because he speaks with power and authority when he really has something to say. Today, he spoke with that deftness that comes about when he finds it necessary to adopt a conciliatory attitude to the house.
This problem has not come about recently. There was a warning issued by the Family Herald on July 4, 1963, and I should like to quote:
Canada faces a serious water shortage. It's threatening the health and pocketbooks of a large part of our population right now and before long it's likely to affect us all in many ways. Within the life time of many readers not only the drier sections of the west but most of Canada will feel the pinch. A big, well-directed conservation and development program, launched right now, could keep a lot of people from being hurt. But any delay will increase the needs and lessen the effectiveness of control measures. Immediate action is urgently required.
This warning came from a responsible magazine, one that has served Canada well for many years. Then, it says:
Although it can be argued that we faced unusually bad weather conditions this year, the fact remains that we are still grappling with a problem which has been created by our expanding population, the rapid advance of industry and agriculture, and modernization of life in the cities and towns and on the farm.

This is a serious and a difficult problem. Mention was made in a most able speech the other day by the hon. member for Brandon-Souris of the action taken by the government of which I had the honour to be the head. We founded the resources for tomorrow conference. It was founded on full co-operation between the dominion and provincial governments. We did not do our consultation in reverse. We did not wait until we found we had entered a field of provincial jurisdiction and then, in a spirit of frustration, have to back up and commence consultations. We brought about a degree of co-operation with all the provinces of Canada that promised well for the future of these resources, which come primarily under provincial jurisdiction although actually have a tremendous effect on the national economy.
One of the most striking statements made by any of the visitors to our country was made to me by the then prime minister of Israel, David Ben Gurion some years ago. His general statement might be summarized in this way: You have a great resource, a resource of particular value in your water, but how you waste it. We have done that. We have polluted our streams, and polluted streams are just as detrimental to Canada's economic future as would be a total absence of water. During the period we were in office we faced the problem of pollution by taking the first, the initial step towards giving assistance to municipalities to provide the necessary measures to meet the pollution problem.
These were steps forward. I do not say that a government can do everything in this regard or a group of governments operating together. But what has this government done? It simply sat, looked at the problem and failed to take any measure whatever of an effective nature. The spirit of resignation could not be better described than it was by the minister in early April-and I have not the quotation before me-when he said the answer to the lakes situation might be to pray for rain. There are many people across Canada today who are beginning to believe that prayer for a change of government might bring a changed attitude towards this problem.
The problem is a tremendous one. It is being faced in all parts of the world. Here in Canada, with the limitless resources we had and which we believed would last for all time, we now find that within a period of three or four decades our country will be a potential dust bowl unless governments act now.
I had hoped that the minister would give us a picture of what the government had in mind, but there was nothing of the kind.

There was simply uncertainty, simply a spirit that the problem is there-"but what can we do about it"? He said the provinces must be consulted, and so they must. In part it is an international problem, but the minister did not give one word concerning the government's plans to meet it. There was just the expression of a pious hope that possibly something will be brought about.
The minister said nothing to indicate that this matter was faced up to at the recent discussions between Canadian ministers and their counterparts in the United States, which were held here in Ottawa. He said nothing to indicate that even small projects are contemplated.
The province of Ontario has made a serious endeavour to meet the problem so far as it can, but it cannot meet a problem which has international and intranational difficulties that must be solved. There was not one word of hope in what the minister had to say.
Some countries are trying to meet this problem by desalinization of sea water. Must we in Canada follow that course? I hope not, but certainly there was nothing but hopelessness in what the minister said today. I saw something of this problem last fall when I was in the Middle East, where they are endeavouring to bring about a solution by breaking down sea water; but the costs are tremendous.
It is estimated that a $840 million nuclear plant could meet the water needs of 3 million to 6 million people. It is also estimated in our own country that within the next 20 years we will have to spend about $5 billions if we are to meet the problem of pollution and the wider problem of the preservation of our water resources. It is a challenge, one that is tremendous in scope. It needs a concept. But what is the concept of the government? After the minister had spoken for a while he finally concluded that to meet this problem, which was so frighteningly described by the hon. member for Simcoe East (Mr. Rynard), the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken) and the other hon. members who have spoken, the whole matter ought to be submitted to a committee of parliament so that briefs might be given thereon.
If the minister had presented some emergent program, something to meet the immediate problems, the larger and more extensive one that will take years to solve could possibly be postponed. But what is going to be done now? What is the situation in Chicago? Is the diversion that is taking place there extending beyond that which is permitted by international agreement? That is a matter upon which we have no information. What a spirit on the part of a government new in office and tired already, overwhelmed, and fearful. Its
Canadian Water Resources members say there is nothing they can do about it and that there are all kinds of constitutional difficulties. Surely there is somebody over there who will say there is some hope that something can be done. Unless there is emergent action taken now, the tremendous tourist traffic Canada enjoys, by reason of the action taken by the Conservative government in the devaluation of the dollar, will be lost and, once lost, not regained.
What of the people engaged in the tourist business? They are actually elevated into space, with their marinas up in the air- occupying a similar position to the government in this regard.
The minister went far afield. He went out to British Columbia. It is a wonderful place to go, a wonderful province; and he went out to the prairies. I say, let us get back to the problem that exists in Ontario and to a lesser degree in Quebec, the problem that is covered by this amendment.
There has never been a government shown so barren of ideas as this one in the address by the minister, assisted during the past two days by two others on the periphery of the cabinet. I ask the government, why are you opposed to the establishment of a national advisory committee to assist in co-ordinating national resource development? Why have you allowed ARDA to become almost a dead letter? A comparison was made by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays), but the figures he gives are meaningless in face of the great opportunities that ARDA provides. If ever a government stood convicted by its defender, that government sits opposite today, for the whole defence consisted of coming before parliament and saying, "Things are bad; they could be worse. They may be worse, but we have not a suggestion of an idea as to what should be done, either by way of emergent action now or for the future." That is not enough.
I am not dealing with the major problem of the future, though it is one that will have to be tackled. These rivers that flow into Hudson bay will have to be reversed and their waters brought into those portions of our country which need them, both because of their industries and their populations. These will be tremendous projects; but what is the hope today for the tourist operator on lake Huron? What hope is there for him in a government that simply points out this is a grave problem, but it has not a suggestion of an idea to deal with it, and that it has to get in touch with the provinces with regard to what could be done? What about co-operative action between the provinces and the dominion? We have not heard one word of what has been done to ensure that the great lakes shall not continue to get lower and lower.

Canadian Water Resources
All we have from the minister is the answer that some years ago the water levels were higher than usual, therefore the fact that they are lower today than they have ever been, and that the trend is downward, is something they have not had time to look into while looking into the other problems they have faced with equal determination and effectiveness. Surely there is someone sitting over there who will rise up and say: These are a few plans we have in mind. The hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dins-dale), the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken), the hon. member for Simcoe East (Mr. Rynard) and others who spoke, placed the problem before the house and asked for action to be taken on behalf of their constituents.
Some people ask: Why do you move a vote of non-confidence on a matter such as this? Well, such votes as this are moved simply in pursuance of the rights of parliament. These votes of non-confidence have been moved throughout the years. Sometimes I read of ministers sitting opposite, together with some of those who are in the outer realms, looking generally to the opportunity to serve in the future in the higher ranks of cabinet posts and saying: Why these votes of non-confidence? I shall not go into that matter now, except to say this, that during the period when we were in office, with the opposition a comparative minority of the house, with one exception in five and a half years every one of the motions to go into supply had an amendment which constituted a vote of non-confidence. How are we to get this matter before the house if we do not follow this course? There is no opportunity to raise it on any other occasion and get the view of the government. We cannot obtain it through questions. Look at the order paper and see the number of questions which remain unanswered, many of them because they represent embarrassment to the government. We cannot bring this up in any other way. Bring it up as a private member's bill, and what happens? It comes, and it goes. Bring it in as a resolution and it is talked out after an hour and goes to the bottom of the list. There is only one way in which the opposition can declare its policies or call upon the government to act in an important matter facing the nation, and that is through the instrumentality of motions to go into supply.
Today, one of the reasons parliament is criticized is because it is said there are so many of these motions. Well, there are no more motions this year, or last year, than there were in every year when we were in office. The only difference is that we spread
[Mr. Diefenbaker.l
them out and people forgot about them, whereas this government brings them along week after week.
