maintopic: FAILURE TO DEVELOP CANADIAN WATER RESOURCES
speechtext: Could we get back to water?

maintopic: FAILURE TO DEVELOP CANADIAN WATER RESOURCES
speechtext:
I am glad of that interruption. The hon. gentleman was not thinking very much about that subject when he was talking about it. He did not at any time address himself to the amendment or attempt to deal with the problem. He simply threw up his hands in a spirit of resignation and indicated to the people of Ontario, of Quebec and of the rest of Canada: This is a tremendous problem and we have not an idea in the world as to what should be done; we have, to all intents and purposes, rendered ARDA nugatory, so what should we do but pray for rain? Laudable as is the recognition on the part of the minister of the power of prayer, we are dealing at the moment with a problem which the government of Canada cannot place on some supernatural level. We want it at this level.
What does the government intend to do? What lies ahead? I listened to the minister and the two other hon. gentlemen who spoke from that side. These were able young men; I like to hear young men going into parliament and making an effective contribution. Those two young men did the best they could, but what a brief they had-nothing to stand on, nothing to answer the amendment, excepting an unusual collection of bureaucratic generalizations brought together with a desire to befog the issue.
All I can say is that here is a problem which is emergent at the moment, a problem which will become national in the years ahead. What action does the government intend to take to meet this emergency? Not one scintilla of evidence has been advanced with respect to a single idea which the government may have on this subject, except to exercise an appeal for guidance from above. The people today are asking this government to give them guidance here and action now instead of this pusillanimous pursuit of uncertainty and evasion.

maintopic: FAILURE TO DEVELOP CANADIAN WATER RESOURCES
speechtext:
When I was listening to the minister delivering his oration and, later, when listening to the observations of the leader of the official opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) I could not help thinking of the story of the old countryman who, when he was asked by a friend if he could read, said: "Well, to tell the truth, I can and I can't". His friend asked: "What do you mean?". "Well," he says, "I tell you. When I sees a sign on the road going somewhere I can read how far, but I can't tell

where to". I thought of that when I was listening to the observations of those hon. gentlemen.
I was impressed by one thing about the speech made by the Leader of the Opposition; I can go away convinced, and tell everyone, that he has a full knowledge of the value of pure water. As far as the minister is concerned-and I listened carefully to what he said-I think he laid greater emphasis on the necessity for prayer than on the need for government policy in this respect, and I support the criticism made by the Leader of the Opposition in this regard. I would judge, from the hon. gentleman's speech this afternoon and from other speeches he has made- and I know he is a person with the best of intentions-that he depends on meetings and press relations without conclusions. He depends on the studies by his officials and by his staff in the water resources branch, without sufficient funds to undertake adequate research. That is a general criticism of his branch. I do not blame the individuals concerned. They can use slide rules and make calculations as well as anyone else. But the water resources branch lacks the funds, lacks the staff, and lacks the support of government policy, plus an over-all plan in cooperation with the provinces, to enable it to do really effective work. I think this is basically the reason we have made so little progress in introducing these programs in Canada as compared with what has been done in the United States.
This is a question which, I think should be treated from a non-partisan point of view and I intend to take my usual position in that regard.
Now I wish to deal with the amendment, Mr. Speaker, which starts out to condemn the government and then concludes as follows:
(3) vigorously continuing and expanding the water and other resources development programs conceived and established by the previous Conservative government.
I do not like that partisan approach to this particular problem. We condemn the government for their activity rather than their inactivity in some respects, but I will come to that later.
Then I come to the subamendment, which is based on the belief of the party supporting it that the question of the development of water resources is a provincial responsibility and is a matter only of provincial concern. We cannot agree with that contention. While we give every support to the ARDA policy and give the former government credit for its introduction, let me truthfully say-I do not want to appear self-righteous because that is not a habit of the members of this
Canadian Water Resources party-that we are the only ones who have had a consistent policy regarding the development and conservation throughout the years of our natural resources, our outlook being based on the over-all philosophy of life with regard to human beings, not on political expediency or the ebb and flow of political tides.
I am rather pleased to see that we have had some influence on the members of the official opposition in view of the fact that the major content of their amendment follows along the lines we have been developing for many years. On behalf of this party, for a period of over ten years I have moved this following motion:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of the creation of a water pollution control division, composed of representatives of the ten provinces, within the framework of the proposed national resources council, with powers and funds required to institute research programs, collect, collate, and analyse water control data, and to co-ordinate the water pollution control objectives for the provinces; in addition, to further the study of water pollution control problems of a national character.
In moving this motion, we in this party recognized the need for an over-all approach to the problem, as well as the need for cooperation between federal and provincial governments. This includes the necessity for a policy which is based on research information and co-operation. For years this motion has been embraced with great affection by members on the government side of the house, without regard to which party they belonged, but the motion was always finally talked out. However, I will give the minister's parliamentary secretary credit in that the last time this motion was debated he agreed that the motion would be referred to the ministers council which was formed after the conference on resources for tomorrow, and I hope those ministers will give some consideration to this aspect of our water resources problem in Canada.
I think it is correct to say that all through the history of Canada, to date, governments on the whole have shown a shocking neglect of the establishment of policies to meet this growing problem effectively. This opinion has been placed on the record repeatedly and I am not going to labour it at this point. However, I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Olson) who made some quite appropriate remarks yesterday on this topic. He dealt with the seriousness of the question, and then as reported at page 2906 of Hansard went on to say this:
Getting back to the question of water, Mr. Speaker, and the preservation and conservation of our water resources, I think it is well for us to consider the position of Canada today in relation to the water resources that we have, and also to

Canadian Water Resources rely on some of the experiences other nations have had, so that we can in fact look into the future and develop programs which will help Canada to avoid these other problems.
I could go on and refer to the figures he quoted regarding the value placed on water in the United States, but I hope that when the hon. member comes to consider other important water problems facing Canada at the present time, including treaties and legislation, he will remember these words and think of the experiences of other nations whose interests were not protected at the time certain arrangements were entered into.
We all know, Mr. Speaker, the basic importance of water for human existence. Quite recently Sir H. Broadley of the United Nations said at a London University lecture:
There is the problem of water supplies; just imagine what quantities of water would be required if all the world adopted our domestic habit of bathing, and at the same time developed factories, atomic energy plants and all other increasing ways for which water is used in great quantities.
In that respect I think the members of this house would be well advised to use their imaginations.
This subject is not a colourful one. It is an important subject but it does not get recognized by the press as one which is, shall I say, colourful enough to justify making a long report about it. There are a small number of the members of our press gallery who are interested in this problem and report faithfully in a few of our newspapers the debates on this important question. I am glad to say that one of these is a young and delightful member of the press gallery, and I hope she makes a very good report of my speech this afternoon.
We have been talking of water in terms of power; but when we think of human existence and human happiness we think of water first of all from the point of view of its domestic use and its consumption by human beings. Second, we think of its recreational values for the enjoyment of human beings; we think of those pleasures that can refresh a man to a far greater extent than attendance at a beer parlour on most occasions, or at a movie show. Then there is the development of fish life and that sort of thing. Next comes industrial uses upon which are based industries from which people earn their livings. Then there is navigation, which is followed by irrigation, the flowing of water on to the soil to produce larger crops which are required to feed the increasing population of the world. Finally there is power production. Over the years we have been able to develop power by various means; but we have never yet discovered a way of producing fresh water in large quantities at economical cost.
[Mr. Herridge.l
The pollution of our streams, the lowering of water levels in the lakes and the lowering of our water tables generally throughout the land, as well as floods in many places and, I am sorry to say-I hope I am forgiven for mentioning this fact-the existence of treaties like the Columbia river treaty, all indicate the great need for a national policy with regard to the conservation and development of our water resources. To indicate the concern in my own district perhaps I might mention a matter which has been of interest to numerous groups throughout the years. I remember when I first came to the house in 1946 receiving letters from Legions in Medicine Hat, Alberta, from the Medicine Hat trades and labour council, from the municipal district of Bow Island and from the water conservation committee of Medicine Hat and Lethbridge, the content of which dealt with the necessity for a water policy and with the great need for canals and the conservation of water to service the thirsty land of Alberta.
This was in 1946. How far have we got along this course? Then we come again to 1949. I remember that the agricultural institute of Canada, of which I have the honour to be a chartered and a life member, presented resolutions to the minister of agriculture of that day urging a similar policy; the need for a national policy for the conservation of our land and water resources. There was a great deal said at that time, but we have not any national policy for the conservation of our water resources today; we have a bits and bobs policy. I am not going to take the time to read the resolution, Mr. Speaker.
Then in 1952 we had the Canadian forestry association dealing with the same problem and mentioning the necessity for a national policy on water conservation. They gave evidence of the depleted water resources found all across our country in dried up streams, lowering water tables, and ever more frequent floods. That was in 1952. It is now 1964 and we still have no national policy with respect to water conservation. Then we come to a conference that was called planning Canada's resources for the future, the first conference of its kind, called by the Canadian forestry association, at the Chateau Laurier hotel, Ottawa, on April 22 and 23, 1954. I attended that conference. There again, Mr. Speaker, there was a discussion of this very important problem. One of the resolutions passed asked for a national policy for the control and development of the nation's water resources. As I said, this was in 1954, and this conference was called as the result of provincial conferences and the activities of other groups. I give credit to the community groups throughout the nation that

have been interested in this problem throughout the years; but if we are going to be effective there has to be leadership at the federal and provincial levels to give effect to a program that will preserve these water resources for the Canadian people.
I want to bring to the attention of the house, Mr. Speaker, a rather unusual situation that occurred recently in .Kootenay West. The people in the Kootenays are concerned with the question of water pollution particularly, and also with the question of the use of the waters of the Columbia basin in Canada for Canadians of this and future generations. I have said that before. They are concerned about pollution. Municipal councils have met and regional groups have met to study this question. On the whole our waters are free of pollution, except in the lower portion of the Columbia river, say from Castlegar to the international boundary. But people are very concerned with the problem of an increase of this pollution and they called in the deputy minister of health for the province. I want to read this editorial to show the approach to this problem on the part of our provincial government. This is an editorial which appeared in the Trail Daily Times, a newspaper that takes a great deal of delight in hammering hell out of me. In this case I agree with what they have to say; I always give credit to my opposition when they say things of which I approve. Just listen to this, Mr. Speaker. This is the approach to this water problem:
We Can't Drink "Averages".
"How do you drink an average?"
It sounded like a joke when it was asked at the annual meeting of the West Kootenay union board of health this week, but there was really nothing very funny about it at all.
The question arose out of a completely inadequate answer given by Dr. James Taylor, the deputy minister of health, to some other questions about the state of the Columbia river.
Dr. Taylor implied that pollution control board secretary Keenan hadn't really meant it when he wrote to the Kinnaird council warning that we were rapidly approaching the point where chlorination would become ineffective as a method of treating Columbia river water.
They are particularly concerned about this because of the tremendous pollution that will occur if the High Arrow dam is built. This editorial continues:
He said that Mr. Keenan's water sample statistics should be regarded from the standpoint of average. Conditions in the river, Dr. Taylor said, "fluctuate".
In other words, chlorinated river water may be "safe" one day and "unsafe" the next; but on an average over a period, statistically the river is "safe".
Unfortunately, the people of the Columbia riverside communities don't drink statistical averages. They drink water-
Canadian Water Resources -like the right hon. leader of the official opposition-
-and it is a bit thick for some hidebound civil servants from Victoria to come in here and try to kid us to believe otherwise.
It is patent nonsense to propose that because the Columbia bacteriological count is well down some of the time and dangerously high at other times, that you can go on to strike a mathematical average and call the water "safe".
The pollution control board and the department of health have got to do better than that.
I mention that, Mr. Speaker, to indicate how they are trying to deal with a question like this which is of such great importance to the people directly concerned. This is another indication of the necessity for federal leadership and some co-ordination of policies. They are getting absolutely nowhere with the provincial pollution control board. They simply come in and hold meetings; they do not take any effective action. This editorial was sent to me and brought to my attention, as a matter of fact, by quite a prominent supporter of the government-and I have some of those as well.
I just want to deal with another aspect of this question and quote from some speeches, copies of which have been sent to me. These speeches were delivered in Portland, Oregon, on November 5, 1963. The first one from which I wish to quote was an address given by Major General W. W. Lapsley before the inland empire waterways association. The title of his talk was "Thirty Years of Water Resource Development", and he said:
As an indicator of future development-we have $1.8 million in the FY 1964 budget for some 35 general investigations, including-
Listen to this. We were told that precedents were not set by the treaty:
-the unprecedented Rampart project on the Yukon river in Alaska.
You see where they are starting. They have already voted money for these investigations. I hope the minister has noticed this, because this money has been voted by the United States senate:
By FY 1966 we will need about $3 million for general investigations. Funds for comprehensive studies of the Willamette and Puget Sound basins are included in the FY 1964 budget and a comprehensive study of the Columbia is authorized.
Here is the interesting quotation from the speech of this well informed American. He is dealing with the Columbia all through the speech, and he said:
The future looks bright. You might even say it looks as if we "have made it"-but don't be too sure.
He was dealing with the procrastination on the part of the Canadian parliament in ratifying the treaty. I want to quote from the remarks of Mr. H. T. Nelson, regional director,

Canadian Water Resources bureau of reclamation, at the 30th anniversary of the inland empire waterways association, Portland, Oregon, on November 4, 1963:
Now let's compare what this economic growth, as illustrated by our experiences on the Columbia river basin project, could mean in future years along the Columbia. Looking at the part of the Columbia river basin along the main stem of the river itself, and up the tributaries to the limits of commercial navigation, we find that there are presently about one and a half million acres irrigated. In future years supplemental waters could be supplied to somewhat over 800,000 acres, and over two million acres of new lands could be brought under irrigation. Just looking at it from a conservation standpoint, in the future we can foresee the irrigation development of from five to six times the area which was actually irrigated on the Columbia basin project in 1962. This would mean, then, that if a similar growth pattern occurred, as was experienced on the Columbia basin project, that there would be a tremendous upsurge in the basic economy of this area.
This is to indicate what they are thinking all the time. You must remember that in this case these gentlemen are talking of the basin to the south of us, the Columbia basin, the states of Washington, Idaho, Montana and California to the south. I am going to requote a paragraph from the Phoenix Gazette of Tuesday, April 7, 1964 which was brought to the attention of the house by my leader last night. The newspaper contains an article dealing with the question of the need for water in Arizona. What does it say?
So this leaves outside sources, and while officially no one would say just where these sources might be, privately some agreed that the huge Columbia river probably would hold best promise of a future supply. Water experts have said the state might possibly get up to 12 million acre feet annually from such a source. The Columbia river is in the Pacific northwest.
You can see how these people are short of water, and I do not blame them for being concerned.

speechtext:
First of all, I am both pleased and surprised, but the minister is quoting national figures. The figures given here are for a very small area of the United States. I want to give a quotation from "Men and Water", a speech made by Senator Henry M. Jackson, chairman, interior and insular affairs committee, at the 30th annual convention of

the inland empire waterways association, Portland, Oregon, November 4, 1963. This is interesting. After talking about what the development of the Columbia will mean to them he says that these are the benefits:
First, and not necessarily in order of importance, by 1980 our present population of about 51 million is expected to increase to about 8 million. While this poses the problem of finding a million new jobs, the very increase in population itself will tend to stimulate economic growth by increasing consumer demand.
This is the Columbia river basin in the United States about which he is talking.
Second, our basic lumber products industry appears to have weathered the worst and is shifting to more sophisticated forest products.
He goes on to refer to refinements in manufacturing and the building of more paper mills. We sell our timber to pulp mills and so far as paper is concerned, allow the processing to be done largely in the United States.
The greater degree of finished processing of northwest forest products offers opportunity for new jobs and, at the minimum, stability in a field that historically has provided our region with two out of every five jobs.
Third, our large and abundant supply of cool, clean water which industry increasingly requires.
Fourth, the ingenuity, resourcefulness and aggressiveness of our northwest citizens in developing new economic opportunity.
Finally, and perhaps most important of all, there is our great supply of low cost hydroelectric power, with more yet to be developed, which provides the lowest cost energy base in the nation for industry.
I have quoted these extracts from this speech made by this gentleman at this most important conference to show that the people there realize what this treaty means to them, what this additional water from Canada means to them in terms of power, in terms of flood control, in terms of irrigation, in terms of jobs, industry and so on.
I think that the conditions we find in Canada in many cases with respect to pollution of our streams, the lowering of our great lakes water levels, the circumstances we find ourselves in with regard to the Columbia treaty and the multitude of investigations that must be done before we can develop our water resources across this country logically and efficiently, indicate more than ever the pressing need for a national water resources policy developed as the result of co-operation between the federal and provincial governments, based on research, based on adequate information, based on an educational program and based on the necessary publicity to inform the Canadian people of what is being done and of the purposes and objectives of such a policy.

Mr. Speaker, in proposing their amendment

and subamendment, the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale) and the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire) both condemned the attitude of the government toward the Agricultural Rehabilitation and Development Act, also known as ARDA. Some members of the opposition, including the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken), the right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) and the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) also referred to ARDA and the government's approach to it.
In the few minutes at my disposal, I should like, in a purely non-partisan frame of mind, to sketch the history of that legislation and describe what happened. It was in June 1961, you will recall, that the house passed the Agricultural Rehabilitation and Development Act. A few months later, the government of the day appointed a director in charge of administration of this legislation, and agreements between the federal and provincial governments were signed in 1962.
Mr. Speaker, I think that we must give credit to the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton), now sitting in opposition, because he was mainly responsible for the implementation of this legislation which, as the Leader of the Opposition pointed out, is perhaps the most interesting legislation passed by both houses under the previous government.
The Prime Minister of Canada has recognized the importance of this legislation and that of rural development. That is why, in February last, he entrusted me with the responsibility of administrating this legislation, and I am proud that, to the responsibilities of the Department of Forestry, the Prime Minister has added those of rural development and, more particularly, the administration of ARDA.
I have been responsible for the administration of that act for two months, and I wish to tell the house how happy I am about this, not only because this piece of legislation offers tremendous possibilities, but also because it is imbued with a spirit that is quite special. It is an act that does not fall within the ordinary framework and which allows the government to accomplish many things with the provinces for the development of rural resources.
It will be remembered also that, at the outset, this act was of an agricultural nature. But it was easily realized that rural problems could not be solved if rural resources as a whole were not dealt with at the same time, that is, forestry, tourists, fishing, the establishment of small industries and the elaboration of policies likely to promote the development of certain rural areas.
Canadian Water Resources
What is known as ARDA constitutes a joint program, which means that it calls for the co-operation of the federal and provincial governments. It is up to the people living in rural areas to take the initiative of suggesting to their respective provincial government programs for the development of their district. Then, provincial governments having approved such programs submit them to the federal government. Therefore, the initiative is not ours. We discuss programs and projects which are submitted to us by provincial governments.
When I assumed the responsibility for the administration of this act, I undertook to visit each and every province in Canada. I think that discussion with provincial ministers responsible for the administration of the act and with provincial officials responsible for its application is the best way to know what they think about the act which, after all, was passed only about three years ago. I also think this is one way of livening up cooperative federalism about which we now hear so much.
Hon. members are aware that the agreements signed with the provinces will expire on March 31, 1965. I hope that, within a few weeks, I will have called on all provincial officials responsible for the administration of that act and that a few weeks later, in June or July, I can hold a meeting with the most interested parties from the provincial and the federal government to review the very basis of that legislation, problems resulting from its administration and improvements that will have to be submitted to the approval of the house next fall.
A few hon. members said that the government had failed to deal with that legislation since coming into power. You will understand that I do not want to indulge in party politics but figures indicate that quite the opposite is true. I do not blame in any way our predecessors, who did not have time to apply that legislation, since it started to operate in the fall of 1962 only, and, as we know, in April 1963 there was a change of government.
The fact remains that since the change in government a great many projects have been approved by the federal government following submissions by the various provincial governments; projects are under way in every province of Canada, and every province is interested in ARDA. To date, 450 projects requiring commitments of $14 million from the federal government have been approved by that government. It would be difficult for me to say exactly how many projects have been approved since the new government took over, but I am under the impression that at least 50 per cent of those projects-

These sums of money have been spent where there were commitments. Many problems still have to be reconsidered, and probably a new direction of ARDA will be proposed to the house. I am not sure yet, because until I have visited all the provinces to discuss with their representatives the application of this act and its consequences on the betterment of standards of living in the
[Mr. SauvS.l
rural class, it will be impossible for me to say exactly what the final direction of this legislation will be.
However, it is clear, since this legislation was discussed during election campaigns, that great hopes have been instilled in rural areas. Quite a few citizens thought that once ARDA was approved, every problem facing the rural classes would be settled. I do not want to criticize anybody. It often happens that, during an election, people become enthusiastic and you feel that, for reasons known to everybody, you have to stress certain hopes which, a few months later, prove impractical.
In most provinces, and more particularly in eastern Canada, farmers and other rural people, who are perhaps not farmers and do not earn their living through farming, would like to see immediate results. People complain that it takes too long to consider and reconsider problems; and I think that, on the whole, they are right to ask for immediate results and the concrete solution of certain problems. To my mind those problems could be immediately solved by the programs devised to improve the various areas.
The people in the rural areas are concerned about what will happen when the studies are completed. As you know, intensive studies are being made in several areas of Canada, but the people wonder if the government will consider its task as completed when the studies are over. I think that we will have the responsibility to show those people that the government is serious when it talks of the development of resources in rural areas.
I also found during my visit that the people were concerned because the authorities had not always succeeded in interesting them in the improvement of their living conditions. In several provinces, they have started to set up organizations of social leaders, that is organizations made up of persons having the responsibility of explaining to the people what ARDA is, what projects are under way, why research is being conducted, why such solution is proposed. The idea is to associate the people living in rural areas with the solution of their problems.
Mr. Speaker, during the first two or three years ARDA has been in existence, it has been found that this legislation really had wide applications. In the interest of the persons concerned themselves, that is people in rural areas who have a low standard of living, it will probably be necessary to restrict the scope of ARDA, in order to actually work for the improvement of living conditions in rural areas.
I do not want to conclude those few remarks without mentioning an exceptional experiment which is now going on in nine

ridings of eastern Quebec-under the supervision of the eastern Quebec development bureau-which is described as a pilot area of ARDA.
There, for almost a year, some 60 persons have been thoroughly studying all the resources in the area and looking for solutions that would improve living conditions of these rural dwellers, who have often been neglected, as we were inclined to solve part of their problems through social security measures rather than through a rational organization of local resources.
The rural development office for eastern Quebec is something unique in this country; it is headed by young economists, sociologists and scientists who, under the direction of the lower St. Lawrence guidance council and the Gaspe peninsula economic guidance council, have endeavoured to find a solution to the local problems.
In a few weeks from now, we will invite members of parliament and newspapermen to come and see for themselves the extraordinary work which is being done in Gaspe in co-operation with the Quebec government and with the approval of both the federal and the provincial governments.
With those few words, Mr. Speaker, I should like to call the attention of the house to ARDA, a truly remarkable piece of legislation which deserves the support of all hon. members, regardless of party affiliation. In my opinion, it offers the means to solve the problem of low income in rural areas.
Obviously, it will be impossible to do so overnight, but within a certain period of time, and with the support of all hon. members, I hope we will be able to improve the condition of rural residents.
Then, people will say that for once we, on the government side, and hon. members of the opposition have unanimously agreed on the need to work together to improve the standard of living of our fellow citizens.

Mr. Speaker, on quite a number of occasions during the past few weeks I have indicated my concern to the house with respect to the great lakes water levels. Some people have failed to understand the importance of this problem and I would direct their attention to the headline in today's Globe and Mail which says, "Government under fire on issue of lake levels." Anything with which the official opposition can hit the front page of the Globe and Mail must have real significance. A further indication of the widespread interest in this problem is a reference to it in the Mount Forest Confederate, a newspaper in a town which is many miles away from the
Canadian Water Resources great lakes area, and many miles from my radio station, but nevertheless it picked up my radio address on water levels in the great lakes and gave it front page headlines. Therefore the problem does have some significance.
The water levels in Georgian bay have become progressively worse over the past three or four years. Early this year indications were coming from reliable sources that the water would reach an all time low in the great lakes, especially in lake Huron and Georgian bay. To build my case, Mr. Speaker, I must present the following evidence so that I can point out something specific.
On March 24 last, as recorded at page 1405 of Hansard, I asked the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Deschatelets) the following question:
If low water levels create a hazardous situation in any harbour on the great lakes, will the minister give the house his assurance that he will give the problem his immediate remedial attention?
The reply was as follows:
Mr. Speaker, I do not follow very well the point the hon. member has in mind, but I am going to look into this matter.
Then on April 6 I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) the following question:
What measures does the government plan to take to cope with the serious low water situation in Georgian bay and lake Huron?
Mr. Speaker suggested that this question go on the order paper. I appealed to the Speaker and said, "This is a serious situation in my riding," but Mr. Speaker insisted that similar questions had been asked. I then put this supplementary question to the Prime Minister:
-owing to the fact that this is a matter of international consequence, has he been contacted by the United States government in respect of this problem?
The Prime Minister replied:
Not to my knowledge, Mr. Speaker. I know it is a serious matter, and if the hon. gentleman would put his question on the order paper, that would give us a chance to make a thorough examination of the matter.
Within a few minutes a note was brought to me from the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Laing) which said that in reply to a question a few days previously he had promised to make a statement on the matter but, owing to the report of his department being incomplete he had asked for further information. When I was in conversation with him later, he promised to bring in a report the following Wednesday or Thursday.
Late during the question period on the following Thursday, when it had become

Canadian Water Resources apparent he would not make a voluntary-statement, I asked him the following question:
Is the minister prepared to make a statement with respect to his findings concerning water levels on the great lakes?
The minister replied:
Our branch officials concerned are finding this a very complex matter. A complete statement is being prepared, and it will be of such length that I think I shall be asking the house to agree that it be printed without being read. However, it is not completed yet.
On April 10, at the conclusion of the four day, semi-annual meeting of the international joint commission, a press release underlined the seriousness of the situation. In the hope that information was available other than the press release, I asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) if he would table the report received by our government from the commission. A day or two later the Prime Minister tabled the report, which was so vague I could hardly believe it to be the commission's release. I have it here, and with the exception of two paragraphs it is chiefly statistics. I would like to put these two paragraphs on the record. The first reads:
As the prospects for this year are not encouraging and supplies in the upper lakes are below normal, the international joint commission and its board of control will direct their efforts to alleviate the effects of low water conditions to the maximum extent possible.
The final paragraph reads:
It feels, however, that all affected interests should be forewarned that notwithstanding the fact that all regulatory works will continue to be operated in accordance with the order of approval, a continuation of the existing drought could result in water supply conditions worse than experienced last year.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I have here a clipping of an article from the Montreal Gazette of April 13, which gives more detail and offers more constructive suggestions. It states that the-
-American co-chairman of the two nation supervisory body, revealed that the levels are the lowest in some 100 years and that a bold, long term approach must be made to divert rivers and streams to feed the lakes and prevent damage that could reach into millions of dollars.
"We need men of vision to consider radical new plans if we are to overcome this adverse cycle of nature" he claimed.
Arnold Heeney, Mr. Roncalio's Canadian counterpart, agreed that the situation is "very bad". Mr. Heeney disclosed that the commission's appraisal of the situation would be forwarded immediately to the two central governments.
This marked the first indication that the situation has reached the stage where the two federal governments might become involved at the top level.
Neither side was willing to disclose details of their report but it was understood the commission informed the governments that no water level improvement is likely this year or next and that the commission will do what it can to minimize any hardships that may occur.

The situation now has alarmed American interests to the point where a committee of 10 senators from states in the great lakes area conferred with their chairman in a special private conference to explore what could be done to alleviate the crisis.
Their chairman informed them the only longterm solution appeared to be one of diverting streams and rivers that feed into Hudson bay or other adjacent areas into the great lakes.
He said there is a limit as to how much diversion would be feasible but some major new plan had to be considered or the lakes basin would face more trouble in the future.
"There is no quick solution in sight," he explained. "We've got to have men of vision and guts to explore sweeping new programs or we will face more hardship and more financial damage in later years."
Then, on April 17, the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, put in his report-a report which was rather in the nature of a review of the situation than a recommendation for relief measures.
The narrow catchment area south of the great lakes has become one of the most heavily populated and highly industrialized parts of the entire world. This applies also to the Canadian side in southern Ontario. The huge inland reservoirs constituted by the great lakes have been treated as though they were inexhaustible, but the toll is becoming more and more evident as the problems of the dwindling flow from the watersheds are multiplied through the drain of increasing consumptive use and the relentless pressure of withdrawals to the water-deficient parts of the Mississippi basin only a short distance to the south.
The situation is forcibly brought home to us in reports such as the following-this one appeared in the March edition of "Ship-Shore", and I should like to quote from it:
It has been estimated that each one inch that the level of lake Huron goes down represents a power loss of $1,000,000 a year, with shipping losses in freight unable to be carried, at a quarter of a million.
Then I have another from the Telegram of April 4, 1964. I should like to put this on record, also.
Big cargo vessels can't get into ports early in the season without cutting tonnage.
Captain Bert Bazelev, fleet manager for Upper Lakes Shipping Ltd., Toronto, says each of the company's 10 large carriers is shipping 1,000 tons light every trip.
It's the same story with other fleets.
Tourist operators, commercial fishermen and cottagers on Georgian bay have literally been left high and dry.
Heavier boats will have to be dragged to water which once lapped at boat houses and docks.
I do not think the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Smith) will have an opportunity to speak. This matter affects his riding and I will, if I may, read the following quotation also from the same paper:

The water is so low at Collingwood that the town's main industry, Collingwood Shipbuilding Ltd., may have to shut down, throwing 1,000 persons out of work.
I have a short quotation here, too, from the Toronto daily Star which I should like to place on record:
Ontario hydro's coal bill is going up. When water levels are low, it has to burn coal to produce electricity at steam generating plants to make up for lost production at hydraulic plants.
Last year it lost 3.5 billion kilowatt hours of production on the St. Lawrence and Niagara rivers, had to buy $13 million worth of coal. In the first three months this year, lost production was 60 per cent higher even than in the same period last year.
My concern, now, is the need for immediate attention to the problem which has arisen in the Owen Sound harbour, affecting in particular the Russel Brothers boatworks in the outer harbour. Russel Brothers have operated successfully in Owen Sound for many years. The original owners are now deceased and the firm was taken over by three employees. These three men found it a large and difficult undertaking to carry on with limited means. Nevertheless, they have managed to keep their staff of 180 men at work. Now they are confronted with the problem of getting new vessels launched. A harbour firefighting tug for Toronto was completed for April for delivery on May 1. Knowing of this delivery date and the condition of the approaches to the plant, I alerted the government with questions on the subject as early as March 24 when I directed a question to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Deschatelets). A few days later I directed a further question to the Prime Minister and, in addition, I spoke privately to two other members of the cabinet. I also got in touch with the district engineer who was familiar with the situation, and in a letter to myself dated April 16, he said:
Thank you very much for your letter of April 13, 1964. The problem of Russel Brothers Limited, Owen Sound, due to low water is indeed distressing. Each mail now brings to my attention a request for assistance in a similar situation. The Georgian bay level is the lowest on record and it is forecast to go even lower. The cost of remedial measures could be monstrous.
I am making a full report to the department on the problem you have outlined and I hope something can be done to relieve it. I share your concern and am giving this matter my personal attention.
I have a further letter from the district engineer dated April 30. Hon. members will note there is an interval of two weeks between the time I received the letter I have just read and the time I got this one.
I have deferred replying to your letter concerning dredging at Russel Bros, at Owen Sound, awaiting word from the department. No word has 20220-187
Canadian Water Resources come yet, nor have funds been authorized for the work. The dredge at Wiarton belongs to Simcoe Dock and Dredge Co.
I had found out that there was a dredge at Wiarton, only a few miles from where this relief work needed to be done, and Mr. Henderson advised me that this dredge belonged to the Simcoe Dock and Dredge Company. The letter continued:
It would be necessary to have the project approved and funds authorized before I could hire a dredge to do the work.
Every day brings correspondence from someone suffering from low water on lake Huron. The water level is at an all-time low and we have a heavy volume of requests for dredging, extension of marine structures, floats, lowering of decks, of docks, etc.

Mr. Speaker, I will continue my remarks at the point I left off before the dinner hour. I called the attention of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Deschatelets) twice to this matter but was informed he was not available. However, a member of his staff said he would have the matter looked up and would call me back. The following day I was informed that the Department of Public Works could not assist. As a last resort I wrote a letter to the Minister of Industry and sent copies to the following ministers: the Minister of Public

Canadian Water Resources Works, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) and the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Mcllraith). I want to read this letter into the record, Mr. Speaker. It is addressed to Hon. Charles M. Drury and reads as follows:
Dear Mr. Minister:
Re: Russel Brothers Limited (Ship builders-Owen Sound)
The low water in the great lakes is having a very bad effect on this industry. Dredging will help, but the officials of the Department of Public Works have informed me that they will not do any dredging because it will benefit only this shipyard. However, unless something is done, the jobs of 180 men in Owen Sound are in serious jeopardy.
The company is required to deliver a fire tug to the city of Toronto by May 1, and they can only move it by building sponsons. I am also advised that they have had to refuse two large repair contracts because of the condition of the approaches to the shipyard.
The amount of dredging required from the shipyard property to the main channel will cost only about $15,000 and the company has offered to pay half of this amount, as a small portion of the dredging will be on its property. The dredging could be done quickly because a dredge is already at Wiarton doing less urgent work.
Having regard to your department's duty to maintain and encourage Canadian industry-particularly in areas such as Owen Sound where alternative employment is not readily obtainable- I would ask you to use your influence to have the Department of Public Works reconsider its decision and allow this industry to continue to provide much needed employment.
To date I have had a reply from only one of these ministers. I should also like to put that reply on the record; it is from the Minister of Transport. I received it yesterday and the letter I sent out was on April 23. Dear Mr. Noble:
Thank you for passing to me a copy of your letter of April 23 addressed to my colleague the Hon. Mr. Drury, asking him, in the interests of maintaining an important Owen Sound industry, to attempt to persuade the Department of Public Works to carry out some dredging in the Owen Sound slip.
What is the rest of it?

That is all there is. We have heard a lot about designated areas and how the government propose to assist. My area might be a borderline example, as it is an area to which it is difficult to attract industry; but surely when the government are presented with an opportunity just to help us hold what we have they will not continue to turn their backs on us. The people of Canada will surely lose confidence in an administration which says one thing and then does another.
To illustrate my point, and especially after the experience I have just related, I should like to quote two excerpts from a speech

made by the Minister of Public Works on May 1, as reported at page 2834 of Hansard. The first quotation is as follows:
I think we should take resolute action to the effect of contributing, through major improvements in strategic sites, to the establishment of important industries, which would have repercussions, not only inside our boundaries, but also with regard to foreign trade.
Then he continued:
A private company told us: If the government agrees to build a wharf, a breakwater or agrees to do some dredging according to the plans submitted, we will build there a plant that will give work to hundreds of people.
I know the house will be interested to know what happened to the Toronto fire tug to which I referred earlier in my speech. When it was evident that the government did not intend to dredge the channel, huge pontoons or sponsons were constructed on which the tug was mounted and floated through the shallow water to deeper water in the bay. These sponsons were then pumped full of water to sink them away from the hull. This operation cost the Russel Brothers boat works quite a large sum of money which they could ill afford to have taken from the limited margin of profit on such a contract. I compliment the management of this plant and their employees for their efforts to keep the plant operating in spite of government neglect.
Owen Sound harbour proper is in need of immediate attention. The grain carrier Agawa arrived at our elevator about two weeks ago and when proceeding to turn around after having unloaded her cargo became grounded. I might say that this elevator has a four million bushel capacity, and on speaking to the manager of the elevator last week end he told me they handled between seven and eight million bushels in one season. Then last week the Canadian oil tanker W. Harold Rea came into Owen Sound with a cargo of oil. She also had difficulty and her draught is only 19J feet when loaded. Under these circumstances how long can we expect shipping to be directed to our harbour?
The Minister of Public Works stated during his estimates that he did not think that dredging could solve the problem. Dredging is a dire necessity in Owen Sound and Colling-wood. This low water level is affecting every aspect of our economy right across this nation. Movement of all commodities by this cheapest of all transportation into our many ports either for use there or for transshipment is so very essential. The tourist industry no doubt will suffer. Our own citizens will undergo many inconveniences. The government has intimated that providence has dealt us a cruel blow and from this they have taken

consolation-and an excuse tor inactivity. Such a phenomenon has happened in other parts of the world and history has proven that men and governments must face up to their responsibilities and implement corrective action.
Many corrective suggestions have been made by previous speakers. The United States government has indicated its alarm, and its willingness to initiate some immediate action on proposals which have been presented to them by their engineers and by a private Canadian engineer. Why does this government not show a little leadership and intestinal fortitude, make their stand known and join with the United States in a joint program and get on with the job that must ultimately be done? The water table throughout much of western Ontario is such that farmers are required to deepen their wells or to drill new ones. The Ontario government has come to realize the great urgency for water conservation and is paying a 50 per cent subsidy toward farm ponds. I have in front of me an excerpt from the London Free Presx which I should like to put on the record at this point:
The provincial government is sending an engineer into western Ontario to assist farmers making plans to alleviate the water shortage.
Further down this article it says:
An expert in water problems, Vernon I. D. Spencer, will assist farmers in the construction of water-catching ponds and reservoirs.
We cannot continue to denude vast areas of our country of forests by timbering and by fires if water levels are to be maintained. In my time I have seen many springs, which were the feeders to our streams and rivers, dry up and cease to exist. Streams that once carried water to the lakes 12 months of the year now dry up after the spring freshet.
I would like to add one more suggestion, Mr. Speaker, to the list already proposed by other speakers. In my opinion reforestation and water conservation in all areas of the great lakes watershed could be enlarged upon. The governments of both the United States and Canada could add much momentum to such a program, where an army of people would be willing to co-operate if given encouragement and direction. This development will have to come eventually, so why not start at the earliest possible time? The population of 40 million in the great lakes area is increasing at a rapid rate and water requirements will have to be met, so it is essential that any plan to conserve water should be carefully considered and, if found to be sound and practicable, should be put into effect. Water must be maintained at satisfactory levels, otherwise circumstances could become disastrous.
Divisions
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I want to say that there are many things we can get along without, but water is not one of them. Water has a multitude of uses; indeed, it is essential to life itself.

DEDUCTIONS FOR CHARITABLE AND OTHER DONATIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the grievance I want to voice tonight in the house concerns the administration of the Department of National Revenue in respect of income tax, and more particularly the receipts for charitable donations which the taxpayers submit to their respective taxation offices throughout the country, and more particularly in our province of Quebec.

subtopic: DEDUCTIONS FOR CHARITABLE AND OTHER DONATIONS
speechtext: In that case, why do you vote with the Liberals?

subtopic: DEDUCTIONS FOR CHARITABLE AND OTHER DONATIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if we all speak at the same time, I think it will be rather difficult to understand each other and to make ourselves heard.

subtopic: DEDUCTIONS FOR CHARITABLE AND OTHER DONATIONS
speechtext: Order, please.

subtopic: DEDUCTIONS FOR CHARITABLE AND OTHER DONATIONS
speechtext:
Some time ago I asked the Minister of National Revenue a question. And I shall quote it as well as the answers which were given to me. The question, which was listed under No. 946, can be found on page 2874 of Hansard. I quote:
1. Does the Income Tax Act provide for a maximum deduction of 10 per cent of net income for charitable donations and, if so, is this provision applied uniformly across Canada?
And the minister's answer was:
1. (a) Yes. (b) Yes.
5, 1964	2951
Deductions for Charitable Donations
That is to say that Canada has a uniform policy which is uniformly applied throughout Canada.
Part No. 2 is as follows:
2.	What procedures do departmental officials follow when processing income tax returns claiming: deductions not exceeding 10 per cent-
1 would ask you to note that under the act, the Canadian taxpayers are entitled to a maximum deduction of 10 per cent of their net revenue for charitable donations.
-and accompanied by receipts for charitable donations?
The answer was as follows:
2.	The amounts claimed as deduction are granted, except if there are good reasons to believe that the submitted receipts are not genuine or that the amounts for which they were made out are mere estimates and not based on any bookkeeping with regard to the sums actually received from each donor by the charitable organization.
Part 3 of the question read as follows:
Are receipts for charitable donations ever questioned and, if so, are deductions ever arbitrarily reduced by departmental officials?
Answer to part 3 of my question was as follows:
3.	(a) Yes. (b) No. Not if it means "without reason". If a charitable organization does not keep books showing the amounts received from each donor, and if the total deduction claimed by all donors is higher than the total amount actually received by the organization, the deduction claimed by each donor may be reduced accordingly.
Part 4 of my question read as follows:
4.	In the reduction of allowances for charitable donations are officials acting within the authority of the Income Tax Act or by some special authority granted to the Minister of National Revenue and exercised with his knowledge?
Answer to said part 4 of my question was as follows:
4.	Within the authority of the Income Tax Act.
Here was part 5 of my question:
5.	What appeal is open to taxpayers who feel that they have been dealt with in an arbitrary manner?
Answer to last part of my question number 946 was as follows:
5. The taxpayer should first of all communicate with the district taxation office and supply detailed information concerning the contributions he actually made to the organization concerned as well as every available evidence or proof thereof. If he is unable to convince the officers of the taxation office that the amounts involved are higher than the deductions granted at the time of assessment he may produce a notice of opposition on form T400A. Two duly filled-in copies of that form should be sent by registered mail, within 90 days of the mailing date of the notice of assessment, to the deputy minister of national revenue (taxation), in Ottawa.
Mr. Speaker, all those answers are given to further confuse the situation and the Canadian taxpayer.

Deductions for Charitable Donations
I have here a bulky record of complaints concerning the treatment received by Canadian taxpayers in my area, in this case, people who had properly filed their tax return, presenting it to the taxation director in Rouyn and claiming exemptions for charitable donations.
For instance, I have here the case of Mr. Roger Dery, of Bourlamaque, P.Q., who wrote me on April 29:
I am forwarding my notice of assessment asking me to pay $12. I earned this year the amount of $3,221.61.
A big salary-
And with my charitable receipts, I had $4 coming back to me. I had charitable receipts in the amount of $200-
That means a little under 7 per cent, around 6 per cent of his net income in charitable receipts.
I had $200 and they cut off $100. So, I would owe them $12. That is not fair with the starvation wages I am getting.
I wrote to the taxation director in Rouyn on May 1, concerning Mr. Roy.
The taxation director, Mr. Merleau, M-e-r-l-e-a-u, a fine bird, replied as follows:
Sir:
He does not even address me as a member of parliament, and he, a government civil servant.
Receipt is acknowledged of your letter dated April 27, 1964 concerning the charitable donations of Mr. Roy.
I regret to inform you that the charitable receipts presented could not be accepted by the Minister of National Revenue-
By the minister, not by himself; the minister cannot accept receipts for $200.
-because the issuer does not keep adequate records.
They went to rectories to see if there was an accounting system, because the government does not have any. I should tell the house right away that all the parish priests in the province of Quebec who are bothered or visited by income tax inspectors should simply throw them out. They should not tolerate them.
-the Minister of National Revenue cannot accept them because the issuer does not keep adequate records.
Would you kindly remember the instructions issued by the deputy minister (taxation) in 1962-
Although the minister cannot accept those receipts, the deputy minister issued instructions in 1962, following the election no doubt-
-which clarify the act on that point for the benefit of charitable organizations which issue receipts for income tax purposes to those making donations. The last paragraph reads as follows:


Charitable organizations which issue receipts for income tax purposes must keep records enabling inspectors to check the authenticity of receipts and the nature of donations.
I shall be glad to have the appropriate corrections made on presentation of any further evidence that the taxpayer might hold to justify his charitable donations.
Mr. Speaker, that letter is probably the most stupid and idiotic I have ever received from a high official of the income tax district office. It requires the taxpayer to supply further evidence, when he sends a receipt in proper form for charitable donations.
The director of the Rouyn income tax district office, the director of the Quebec district and those of the other districts throughout the country, the minister himself, in brief everybody knows that I do not mean charitable donations that we give only on Sunday collections at church. There are many charitable organizations which request our help, week after week and day after day. Those are the boy scouts, the ladies of Ste. Anne, the children of Mary; it is a tag-day here, a tag-day there, the Richelieu club, the foreign missions, ail kinds of organizations which ask for our help the year round. We give 50 cents, a dollar, two dollars, but we do not keep a record of all those sums.
I have here the example of a workman, under 21 years of age, who earns $3,221 a year, a married man with children. He files his income tax return, sends a $200 receipt for charitable donations, and the director of the Rouyn income tax office decides, in an arbitrary way, to cut this receipt by $100 and claim from him an amount of $4 instead of refunding to him the $12 to which he was entitled.
Mr. Speaker, this is a great shame for us, federal members of parliament, to face our electors concerning the arbitrary enforcement of the Income Tax Act. That is why we ask the minister and the officials of the department whether, in the Income Tax Act, it is stipulated that every citizen is entitled to a maximum deduction of 10 per cent of the net income for charitable donations. If the answer is in the affirmative it should be applied and all Canadian taxpayers should be granted a maximum of 10 per cent for charitable donations, and charitable organizations, parish priests, ministers, the Salvation Army or any other welfare organizations should be left alone. A taxpayer should not be asked if he can explain a certain amount or whether he has some special system of accounting to please the income tax deputy minister or the director of the Rouyn district income tax office or any other district office in Canada.
I have another letter from Bourlamaque which reads as follows:

Sir, I am sending you my notice of my assessment. According to my income tax return, I was entitled to a refund of $102.15. The $200 deduction which I claimed for charitable donations has been reduced to $100.
Another $100 cut.
So, I got only $80.15. There is still $22 coming to me.
Mr. Speaker, why be mean with people who earn their living by the sweat of their brow and who are not entitled, like business owners, to deduct from their income tax the cost of their equipment and of their working material?
Doctors, dentists, lawyers, garage operators are entitled to deduct from their income tax the cost of the material they purchase, and of the machinery or equipment they need. We have the right to deduct such costs from our taxable income, whereas the poor miners, the labourers and the mechanics who buy equipment for hundreds of dollars are not entitled to deduct from their taxable income the cost of the tools they use to earn their living by the sweat of their brow.
Not only are they deprived of the right to do so, but even the amount of income tax that they must pay each year is increased, especially since last year.
Mr. Speaker, we strongly object to that arbitrary attitude taken against the Canadian taxpayer, the man who earns his living by the sweat of his brow-

It is not our system, it is yours and I am against it. But at least, I have enough pluck to fight against it.
Mr. Speaker, if there are that many blockheads we will have to shut them up.
In any case, the district income tax director of Rouyn wrote another letter similar to the one I referred to earlier, that is in exactly the same terms. This time, he did not have his letter photocopied; it is the original. There again, he writes:
Charitable organizations giving income tax receipts must have a bookkeeping system which permits tax inspectors to verify the authenticity of the receipts and the nature of the donation.
I shall be pleased to cause appropriate corrections to be made on submission of supplementary evidence which the taxpayer may have in order to justify his charitable donations.
I hold in my hand a letter from a taxpayer of Sullivan in which he says:
I am sending my income tax papers for 1964. X have no receipts I can send you to prove anything, because the government has all my receipts for charitable donations which amount to $250.
And there again, a notice of assessment was sent to him from which I quote a paragraph:
Your deduction for charitable donations has been reduced to the amount deductible according to the admissible receipts produced.
There was only one receipt involved in the amount of $250, but according to the admissible receipt produced, which was refused, these charitable donations amounted to $250. They were reduced from $250 to $100. And while the taxpayer had claimed a refund of some thirty odd dollars, he is now asked to pay the sum of $12.80.
That is a taxpayer who, in 1963, earned $3,540. When he is asking for an exemption on $250 in charitable contributions, what does that mean? About 6i or 7 per cent of his taxable income.
Here we have a family whose income for a 12 month period amounted to $3,540, and the head of the income tax district office decides, just like that, to take $20 away from it.
And the same thing happens over and over again in all fields of activity.
2954	HOUSE OF
Deductions for Charitable Donations
I have here a letter from Mr. Gilles Le-jeune, of Bourlamaque, who claimed an amount of $250 in charitable donations.
He was allowed a deduction of only $100, and the income tax officials took a similar arbitrary attitude.
I have a letter from another elector from Val d'Or. Everyone knows that you do not need to produce receipts if you claim only a $100 deduction. Why bother about that then?
In fact, is there anyone in Canada who does not give to charity, one way or the other, at least $200 a year? As I said a while ago, we are constantly besieged with request for assistance to the poor and the needy. Requests for help to needy children, to the destitute, etc. come right and left from organizations like the Federation des femmes canadiennes-frangaises.
Mr. Speaker, I have in my hand a letter from Mr. Andre Cartier, of Val d'Or, who writes to me as follows:
Dear Mr. Caouette,
I am writing to you about my income tax return. I was supposed to get a reimbursement of $55.40 but I have received only $19.40. I submitted a receipt of $350 for charitable donations but it was cut down to $100.
The situation is the same for all Canadian taxpayers, but I wonder to what extent that discrimination is restricted to certain counties of the province. Could it be that the counties which elected a government member are less affected by that cut in charitable donations than those which elected an opposition member? I wonder.
I know that our friends opposite are also confronted with such problems and that they were faced with several such claims, but is this arbitrary action carried to the extreme in their county as it is in ours, that is the counties represented by opposition members?
Mr. Speaker, I would also like to quote another letter from Bourlamaque:
As you have suggested this afternoon in Val d'Or, I am forwarding the notice of assessment I received from the income tax division-
-Income $4,652.03-
Personal exemptions, $2,900.
Medical expenses-
His charitable donations were reduced from $250 to $100, that is less than 5 per cent of his net income.
This inspector-I mean the director, Mr. Merleau, that is the dictator-replies again:
Your statement for charitable donations-
It is always the same letter. Why? All he can say is that the minister cannot accept the receipt, that in 1962 the deputy minister has given instructions to the inspectors to check the accounting of parish priests and of charitable and welfare organizations in Canada.


Therefore, Mr. Alphonse Marcotte's charitable donations were also cut down to $100; he lives in Bourlamaque.
Another taxpayer, Mr. Octave Mercier, who earns $3,894 per annum and who submitted a statement for charitable donations amounting to $207.50-which does not even represent 6 per cent of his annual income-also had his charitable donations chopped down to $100.
All members of the house could say the same thing, for we all get similar complaints from our voters, the Canadian taxpayers.
That is why, Mr. Speaker, in the grievance I am making tonight, I would like to submit to the minister that income tax inspectors-be they Mr. Merleau, of Rouyn, Mr. Gingras, of Quebec, Mr. Audet, of Quebec, or whoever they may be-should not be authorized to go and investigate in our parochial presbyteries.
The minister should see that the legislation now in effect is applied, that the provisions of the said legislation are enforced and that their application is generalized throughout the country. It would be less expensive for the department to make refunds to Canadian taxpayers than to pay those inspectors who call at rectories and make the Canadian taxpayer ridiculous by compelling him to comply with provisions which he cannot understand. For instance, they say that the taxpayer should provide further evidence, when the income tax inspector knows very well that there is no other evidence for those charitable donations than the receipts filed with the local or district income tax office.
Mr. Speaker, the government should show more concern for the Canadian taxpayers. Some people who hardly earn $3,000, $3,500 or $4,000 per year are pestered by income tax inspectors when they are already hard put to manage their budget or are unable to make ends meet.
Why allow those people to be tormented any longer by income tax bureaucrats who refuse to pay them amounts as ridiculously low as $4, $12, $25, or $30? They would spend that money on groceries and it would increase their purchasing power.
But no. The government swallows everything at the expense of the small taxpayer and the low wage earner. We shall never protect those people enough, because, as I said earlier, they deserve the attention of the Minister of National Revenue. There is discrimination against the little people who have trouble keeping alive under the present system.

When the minister orders his officials to grant the 10 per cent deduction for charitable donations, he will make things much easier for present as well as future administrators.
It is in the name of those workers, miners, labourers, small wage earners, white or blue collar workers that we protest tonight against that arbitrary way-and I will never say it often enough-in which income tax inspectors and directors treat the Canadian taxpayers.
Let us try to take a stand, once and for all, and solve those problems in order to stop complaints from our own electors about such discriminatory measures taken against them by an administration which I would call fundamentally dishonest.
When we have won on that point, Mr. Speaker, we will not endeavour to get credit for it. The Minister of National Revenue can take credit for it; let us stop, as I said, torturing workers in our area and in the province.
I have also before me a letter from Mr. Germain Houde, of Bourlamaque, whose receipts were cut down to $100.1 have another one from Mr. Albert Santerre, 1 Main street, Sullivan, in Abitibi, whose receipts for charitable donations were cut down to $100, whereas it is stipulated in the guide accompanying the T4 form that everyone is entitled to $100 deduction. We do not need a Mr. Mercier or a Mr. Merleau, of Rouyn, to tell us how to fill our forms. We know how.
I have also a letter from Mr. Rosaire Tousignant of Val d'Or, who claimed $300 for charitable donations which were cut down to $100. Why? Because an income tax inspector was not satisfied with the accounting system and because the minister refused to accept the receipt, according to what Mr. Merleau wrote to me on May 1.
The charitable donations of Messrs. Stanislas Tremblay, Sullivan and Conrad Godin, of Val d'Or, were also cut down to $100. It is always the same thing. At least, they could save on all this paper which is paid for by the workers.
Why not merely say, whenever the opportunity arises for the minister to make a speech, that from now on, nobody can claim more than a $100 exemption for charitable donations, since we do not believe any more in the parish priests, the ministers or the welfare associations in this country? Why should we question the sincerity and honesty of people such as parish priests and ministers? Moreover, why should we question the Canadian taxpayer's honesty?
Deductions for Charitable Donations
Could it be, by any chance, that the income tax inspectors and directors that we have today in Canada are nothing but thoroughly clever people whose only wish is to preserve Canada's economy by swindling and robbing further the Canadian worker?
Mr. Speaker, there are limits to injustice. The minister will have to answer for his many injustices to Canadian workers if he is not willing to answer at this time. Those people should be treated with a little more respect by income tax district offices, and when they submit a proper receipt, signed by a parish priest or a charitable organization, it must be remembered that in addition to the donations vouched for by the receipts, there are often other large amounts which are given occasionally, as I said at the beginning of my remarks, when parties are held by parish, local and other organizations in order to help the very poor.
Mr. Speaker, I ask the minister to make a statement as soon as possible, not in favour of income tax directors and inspectors, income tax deceivers and blood suckers, as I call them quite often, but in favour of the Canadian workman, the day labourer who is tired of being fleeced the way he is at present.

No, Mr. Speaker, I will not allow it.
The officials of the Department of National Revenue apply the provisions of the legislation. It is essential that the legislation be amended by the government to make it more flexible and meet the needs of the Canadian taxpayer since the great majority of Canadian workers are now complaining about the provisions of the Income Tax Act.
The hon. member for Villeneuve suggested that 10 per cent should be deducted automatically without any consideration. I would prefer that the government amend the act and automatically deduct an amount of 10 per cent up to a $500 maximum, because otherwise, it is the people from the more prosperous provinces, enjoying the higher incomes in Canada and living mostly in the provinces of British Columbia and Ontario who would benefit from it and, by the same token, if the government were to carry out the suggestion made by the hon. member for Villeneuve, it would discriminate against the people from Quebec and the maritimes who have a lower average income than those from British Columbia and Ontario. This would be necessary in order to avoid any criticisms.
Often, that is, most of the time, the Department of National Revenue rejects receipts for charitable donations without any explanation.
As far as I am concerned, whenever a constituent submitted his case to me and I made representations on his behalf to the Department of National Revenue, most of the time I got satisfactory replies. But in order to prevent electors from coming to their member's office, which is not normal in such cases, I feel it would be advisable to amend the act and make it more flexible.
I trust that the Minister of Justice will put pressure upon his colleague so that this act will be amended and brought more in line with the best interests of the Canadian people.
It is not normal that hundreds of complaints should be made across the country against the Income Tax Act, especially by people in the low income brackets. I feel some discrimination really exists and that this legislation should be made more flexible in order to comply with the wishes of the population.
There is one thing I cannot tolerate, and I refer to those raids carried out by employees of the income tax division, acting on the instructions of their superiors, upon members of the Canadian clergy. That, I submit, results in weakening the authority of our clergy. It is not normal that income tax employees


should be allowed to question the value of our clergy across Canada by submitting them each year to numerous raids and visits on all sorts of pretences.
I think the act or rather some of its provisions should be changed, adapted and made to conform to the requirements of the Canadian people.
Consequently, in view of the numerous complaints made throughout the country, I believe it is the duty of the government to take the necessary steps to correct the flaws existing in that field.
I heard some members on the government side make certain remarks. I would be very pleased if at least one of them would take the floor, after me, and say, according to his conscience, whether he approves of the visits made to presbyteries across the country and is happy to see the disappointment of the working class in regard to the manner in which income tax returns submitted by the Canadian workers are treated. I would be particularly pleased to hear the hon. member for St. Jean-Iberville-Napierville (Mr. Dupuis), or the hon. member for Levis (Mr. Guay) or the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Choquette). If they are really aware of their responsibilities, they will take the floor, after me, to say what they think of the act and make appropriate suggestions to the government so that the latter may implement the promises it made to the Canadian people during the last election campaign.
